body.heading: Three rules for everything that moves
paragraphs: Newton's first law says an object keeps doing what it is doing — resting, or moving in a straight line at a steady speed — unless a force acts on it. This stubbornness is called inertia. Things do not stop or swerve by themselves; something must push or pull them.

The second law links force, mass and acceleration: the same push accelerates a light object much more than a heavy one. The third law says forces come in pairs — when you push on something, it pushes back on you with equal strength in the opposite direction.

body.heading: The laws on the road and in the kitchen
paragraphs: A seatbelt exists because of the first law. When a car brakes hard, the car slows down, but your body tries to keep travelling at the old speed. The belt supplies the force that slows you with the car, instead of the dashboard doing it.

Walking is the third law in action. Your foot pushes backwards on the ground, and the ground pushes forwards on your foot — that answering push is what actually moves you. On ice the first push fails because there is too little friction for the ground to push back with.

body.heading: Why spaceflight runs on Newton
paragraphs: Above the atmosphere there is almost no friction or air resistance, so the first law rules completely. A spacecraft that fires its engine for a minute and then shuts it off will coast for years — which is how probes launched in 1977 are still travelling outward today.

Rockets climb by the third law: they throw exhaust gas violently downwards, and the gas throws the rocket upwards in return. No air or ground is needed to push against — the pair of forces between rocket and exhaust does all the work.

description: Three short rules describe nearly every push, slide and crash in daily life — here is each law wearing ordinary clothes.
